title: Trained 210M text-to-image model from scratch on one GPU: what actually mattered
gist: Ivan Mikhnenkov trained tinydit, a 210M-parameter diffusion transformer, from scratch in 3.5 days on a single RTX PRO 6000 over 4.2M images at 256 resolution, reaching FID 27.0 and 90% object accuracy while riding on a frozen FLUX.2 autoencoder and flan-t5-base text encoder. His ranked conclusions invert conventional priorities: data curation mattered more than architecture, the training loss barely moved (0.805 to 0.754) while output quality went from blobs to photographs, torch.compile delivered 2.4x speed and half the memory on the training step, and a timestep shift of 2.8 matched to the 32-channel latent mattered more than doubling sampling steps.

insights.claim: A 210M-parameter diffusion transformer was trained from scratch in 3.5 days on a single RTX PRO 6000 over 4.2M images at 256 resolution, with the transformer, training recipe, data pipeline and evaluation all written originally and only the FLUX.2 autoencoder and flan-t5-base text encoder taken frozen off the shelf.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Credible text-to-image training now fits in a single-workstation budget when the encoder and autoencoder are borrowed — the moat is shifting from training compute toward data curation and the frozen component ecosystem.
insights.quote: a 210M-parameter diffusion transformer trained from scratch in 3.5 days on a single RTX PRO 6000, on 4.2M images at 256²
insights.locator: I wanted to deeper understand how modern image generation works

insights.claim: The training step ran at 0.76 seconds and the full run was 400k steps at batch 256, a throughput figure that makes the entire economics of the experiment auditable.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Concrete per-step cost lets others price equivalent runs against cloud GPU rates and judge whether owning hardware beats renting for this class of work.
insights.quote: 0.76 seconds per step; 400k steps in 3.5 days.
insights.locator: The rest. AdamW at 2e-4

insights.claim: The author's ranked conclusion is that the data decided the outcome before training started, and an earlier scaling attempt using a recaptioned web crawl of about a million images produced a model worse than training on COCO alone because the images were random internet quality and the captions did not match them.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: More data actively destroyed quality — direct evidence against naive scaling and in favor of curation-heavy pipelines, which raises the value of licensed, clean, well-captioned image corpora.
insights.quote: It made the model worse than COCO alone
insights.locator: 1. The data decided the outcome

insights.claim: The winning selection method was manual: pull twenty real rows from every candidate dataset, view them exactly as a 256-resolution model would, and only then choose — a step the author says decided more than any architectural choice.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: A cheap, repeatable diligence step that beats automated quality filters; useful heuristic when evaluating any team's claimed data advantage.
insights.quote: Twenty real rows per candidate, on one page, decided more than any architectural choice.
insights.locator: 6. Five things I would tell someone

insights.claim: The final mix was 60% Pexels stock photos (2.8M images, captioned by Qwen3-VL-30B and CogVLM), 25% the Aesthetics subsets of FLUX-Reason-6M (1.2M images, filtered by quality score), and 15% COCO 2017 train (118k images with GPT-4V and human captions).
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Shows the current open-source stack: licensed stock imagery as the backbone, VLM-generated captions as the labeling layer — VLM inference is now a required input cost of any image-model training run.
insights.locator: The mix that trained this model

insights.claim: Synthetic images were deliberately capped at a quarter of the mix on the explicit reasoning that a model fed mostly generated images learns the generator's look rather than the real distribution.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: A concrete ceiling on synthetic-data substitution in the image domain, which limits the 'synthetic data solves the data wall' thesis and keeps real-imagery licensing valuable.
insights.quote: a model fed mostly generated images learns the generator's look
insights.locator: Three details did real work

insights.claim: Caption length is sampled per training step — the long caption 50% of the time, the short one 40%, and an empty caption 10% for classifier-free guidance — because long-only captions hurt short prompts while short-only captions hurt composition.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Caption-length distribution at train time directly determines prompt-length robustness at inference — a mechanism explaining why some models collapse on terse user prompts.
insights.quote: long-only captions hurt short prompts, short-only captions hurt composition
insights.locator: Three details did real work

insights.claim: A naive near-square filter would have discarded 94% of COCO and 99% of Pexels because real photography is 4:3 and 3:2, making square-crop pipelines a massive silent data destroyer.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Quantifies how much usable training data conventional preprocessing throws away — a 99% loss rate is the kind of inefficiency that reorders dataset economics.
insights.quote: A naive "keep only near-square images" filter would have discarded 94% of COCO and 99% of Pexels
insights.locator: That last point deserves its own paragraph

insights.claim: Training used five aspect-ratio buckets of roughly 256 tokens each (256×256, 288×224, 224×288, 320×208, 208×320) with each batch drawn from a single bucket from the very first step, mean crop of only 3 to 5% of the long side, and 2D rotary embeddings supplying position so the transformer needs no per-shape change.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: 2D RoPE makes multi-resolution training nearly free architecturally, removing the historical excuse for square-only pipelines.
insights.locator: Instead the model trains on five aspect-ratio buckets

insights.claim: The bucketed model generalizes to a 448×256 frame it never saw during training, indicating the position encoding rather than memorized resolutions carries shape handling.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Resolution extrapolation from a small training budget means aspect-ratio flexibility need not be bought with more compute.
insights.quote: it even generalises to a 448×256 frame it never saw
insights.locator: Position comes from 2D rotary embeddings

insights.claim: The square-crop warm-up phase common in image-model training is characterized as a habit rather than a requirement, discarding exactly the parts of the frame that captions describe.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Identifies inherited convention as an active source of caption-image mismatch — a cheap correction for anyone running an image-training pipeline today.
insights.quote: The square-crop warm-up phase is a habit, not a requirement
insights.locator: 6. Five things I would tell someone

insights.claim: The transformer contains nothing invented — DiT with cross-attention to text tokens in the PixArt and SANA lineage, 2D RoPE, QK-normalisation, SwiGLU feed-forwards and adaLN-single modulation — and the author treats that convergence as the point rather than a shortcoming, noting FLUX and SD3 use joint attention instead.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Image-model architecture has commoditized into a standard block; differentiation has moved to data, recipe and evaluation, which is where competitive advantage should now be assessed.
insights.quote: Nothing in the transformer is invented here, and that is the point
insights.locator: 2. The architecture is the current recipe

insights.claim: Switching to adaLN-single modulation — one shared modulation network plus a small per-block table instead of a full linear per block — freed 27% of the previous parameter count at zero compute cost, and that budget was reinvested into depth at 896 width, 16 blocks and 14 heads.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: A 27% free parameter reallocation shows how much of a small model's budget goes to conditioning plumbing rather than capacity — relevant to every on-device generative model design.
insights.quote: That change alone freed 27% of the old parameter count for zero compute
insights.locator: 2. The architecture is the current recipe

insights.claim: Sixteen learned register tokens join the image sequence at block 3 and are dropped before output, and every cross-attention block gets two learned always-attendable null key/value slots, giving the model somewhere to park global state and to 'attend to nothing'.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Register tokens migrating from vision transformers into diffusion transformers in 2026 is a concrete example of technique transfer that a solo builder can adopt immediately.
insights.locator: The one addition from recent research is registers

insights.claim: Attention instrumentation confirms the registers work as intended: at mid-noise in a middle block the two null slots receive about 90% of cross-attention mass, the end-of-sequence token that previously acted as the attention sink drops to 4%, register vectors grow to 4-13x the norm of an image token, and each image patch routes 8-18% of its self-attention to them.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Rare quantitative evidence of the attention-sink pathology and its fix; the 90%-to-null-slots figure implies most cross-attention capacity was previously being wasted on a hijacked token.
insights.quote: the two null slots receive about 90% of all cross-attention mass; the end-of-sequence token, which used to be the sink, gets 4%
insights.locator: It worked, and measurably

themes.theme: Recipe: noise schedule, auxiliary losses, compile

insights.claim: A rectified-flow timestep shift of 2.8 is required because the FLUX.2 latent has 32 channels rather than 4 — an image stays recognisable at noise levels that would have destroyed a 4-channel SD latent, so more noise is needed to pose equally hard high-noise problems.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Latent channel count dictates the correct noise schedule; teams swapping in a modern high-channel autoencoder without re-tuning the shift will under-train exactly where layout is formed.
insights.quote: A 32-channel latent wants a shift near 2.8; without it the model under-trains exactly where layouts are formed.
insights.locator: 6. Five things I would tell someone

insights.claim: With the shift applied, half of all training samples sit above 74% noise and 15 of the 20 sampling steps land in that region, which is where image layout is decided.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Quantifies that the majority of both training and sampling budget goes to the high-noise layout phase, not to detail refinement — a useful lens for where quality bottlenecks live.
insights.locator: 3. The recipe: a shift, two extra losses

insights.claim: Two auxiliary losses were added: a cosine term on velocity direction from LightningDiT, because at high noise MSE is dominated by magnitude while direction determines the image, and a dispersive loss on block-5 features from Wang and He (2025) that pushes different samples' internal representations apart without any external encoder and costs nothing.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Both are free-to-compute additions addressing known failure modes (magnitude-dominated loss, representation collapse) — low-risk upgrades for any flow-matching training stack.
insights.locator: Two auxiliary losses

insights.claim: torch.compile is misclassified as an inference tool: applied to the training step it delivered a measured 2.4x speedup and half the memory, because Dynamo traces the forward, AOTAutograd derives the backward and Inductor fuses elementwise operations around the matmuls in both directions, at the cost of static shapes requiring one compiled graph per bucket.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: A 2.4x training speedup with half the memory from a compiler flag is the cheapest capex avoidance available; widely underused, and it reduces the GPU count needed for a given research plan.
insights.quote: Compile the training step. It is the cheapest 2× you will ever get.
insights.locator: 6. Five things I would tell someone

insights.claim: The EMA decay was set to 0.9999, a 10,000-step horizon, on the argument that the commonly used 0.999 is far too short for a 400k-step run, alongside AdamW at 2e-4 with betas (0.9, 0.95), fp32 master weights under bf16 autocast, and linear LR decay to zero over the final quarter.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Default hyperparameters copied from short runs silently degrade long runs; EMA horizon should scale with total steps.
insights.locator: The rest. AdamW at 2e-4

themes.theme: Loss is not quality: evaluation discipline

insights.claim: The flow-matching loss fell only from 0.805 to 0.754 across the entire run while outputs went from blobs to photographs, because at high noise many image-and-noise pairs are consistent with a given input, making most of the loss an irreducible floor and leaving only a thin learnable layer on top.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Loss curves are structurally uninformative about generative quality — a warning for anyone underwriting model progress from training dashboards or vendor loss charts.
insights.quote: The flow-matching loss fell from 0.805 to 0.754 over the whole run while the images went from blobs to photographs.
insights.locator: 4. The loss is not the signal

insights.claim: Loss is still useful as a health signal specifically because training and held-out loss stayed equal to the third decimal place throughout, which is how the author knows nothing was memorised across 24 epochs of the data.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: A clean, cheap memorization check — directly relevant to copyright exposure claims about image generators trained on real photography.
insights.locator: 4. The loss is not the signal

insights.claim: Quality was tracked every 10k steps on a frozen caption set using FID, FD-DINOv2, an 80-class COCO-detector object accuracy on 'a photo of a {class}', and the PickScore and HPSv2.1 human-preference models, with results moving from FID 33.7 / FD-DINOv2 570 / 65% object accuracy at 10k steps to FID 27.0 / 218 / 90% at 400k.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: A concrete multi-metric evaluation harness that others can copy; the numbers also set a public baseline for what 210M parameters at 256 resolution buys.
insights.locator: Quality was tracked every 10k steps

insights.claim: The metrics saturate at different times — FID and object accuracy plateaued around step 300k while FD-DINOv2 and the preference scores kept improving to the end, with learning-rate decay over the last 100k steps alone buying a further 5% on FD-DINOv2.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: FID saturating early while human-preference metrics keep climbing means FID-based leaderboards understate late-stage progress — a reason to distrust single-metric model comparisons.
insights.locator: FID and object accuracy saturated around step 300k

insights.claim: The preference models used for tracking, PickScore and HPSv2.1, are explicitly the same family that will be used as rewards in the planned reinforcement-learning phase, deliberately aligning the evaluation metric with the future optimization target.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Metric and reward converging is efficient but invites reward hacking — worth watching whenever a lab reports gains on the same preference model it optimizes against.
insights.locator: Quality was tracked every 10k steps

insights.claim: Measured on 2,456 held-out prompts, raising sampling from 20 to 50 steps is worth only 0.4 FID and nothing on preference scores, while removing the training-time timestep shift costs more than doubling the step count gains.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Training-time schedule design beats inference-time compute for this model class — the cheaper lever is upstream, which matters for anyone pricing per-image inference cost.
insights.quote: 50 steps instead of 20 is worth 0.4 FID and nothing on the preference scores; removing the training-time shift costs more than doubling the step count gains.
insights.locator: Measured on 2,456 held-out prompts

insights.claim: Sampling trajectory inspection shows the image layout is fixed after three steps and everything afterward is sharpening, explaining mechanistically why 20 steps suffice.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: If composition is decided in the first three steps, early-step compute allocation and distillation targets should concentrate there — relevant to fast-sampler design.
insights.quote: the layout is fixed after three steps and everything after that is sharpening
insights.locator: One more figure, because it explains

insights.claim: The model reliably handles single objects, animals, scenes, colours and simple spatial relations across all five aspect-ratio shapes, but fails on readable text, close faces, crowds, counts above three, clock hands and stacked geometry — the stated known limits of 210M parameters at 256 resolution.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: A published failure grid gives a clean capability floor for small image models, useful for judging when a commercial product's claims imply genuinely larger models.
insights.quote: Readable text, close faces, crowds, counts above three, clock hands, stacked geometry.
insights.locator: 5. What it can and cannot do

insights.claim: The author argues a failure grid belongs in every write-up of this kind, positioning explicit negative-capability disclosure as a norm the field should adopt.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: Norm-setting against cherry-picked demo reels; a useful diligence question to put to any generative-model vendor.
insights.quote: here is the failure grid, which I think belongs in every write-up like this
insights.locator: 5. What it can and cannot do

insights.claim: The base model was deliberately left undistilled and on plain classifier-free guidance so that the next phase can be reinforcement learning with Flow-GRPO, using the tracked preference models as rewards and the failure grid as the explicit target list.
insights.speaker: Ivan Mikhnenkov
insights.so_what: RL post-training is migrating from language models into diffusion models; if Flow-GRPO fixes documented failure modes at 210M scale, it changes the capability-per-parameter curve for image generation.
insights.locator: What's next
